<reason>Both sides opened well and stayed epistemically clean with real examples (Maya Bay, Fjaðrárgljúfur, Jackson Hole, Amsterdam). PRO's "turn down the amplifier, both-not-either" frame and friction argument were genuinely strong. But CON won the decisive clash it set up: once PRO conceded geotag limits are a complement, the burden became showing the complement adds something capacity tools don't. CON answered PRO's gateless-sites pressure with concrete gateless tools (exit closures, shuttles, fences, permit parking) and forced a costly concession with the fork question — PRO admitted the motion "reaches the selfie," transforming it from "commercial-scale promotion" into government-requested edits of ordinary visitors' posts, which CON weaponized as both broader and weaker than advertised (unenforceable request to Meta, coordinate rebuilt by evening, visitors blinded). PRO's answer to "name one site where promotion limits alone worked" was to call the question rigged and re-cite Amsterdam, which CON had already neutralized as a destination controlling its own voice. CON's "one tool hits the number with certainty, the other hopes" and "a tool that stops no feet is free, the way doing nothing is free" framed the weighing memorably. Clips cost CON slightly (two clipped turns vs PRO's one) but only tail flourishes were lost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2: after PRO's pressure answers, B showed gateless sites already have enforced gateless tools that "hit the number on the day it is enforced," then converted PRO's A1 concession ("yes, it reaches the selfie") into the debate-deciding point — a speech-editing apparatus aimed at ordinary people, dependent on platform goodwill — while PRO never recovered a real-world case where pin removal alone reduced traffic.</best_rebuttal>
